title: Numbers 1-10
description: Count from zero to ten, count things and count people.

guide.title: Counting things
guide.text:
The numbers one to ten are ondu, eradu, mooru, naalku, aidu, aaru, elu, entu, ombattu, hattu. Watch the vowel lengths: mooru and aaru are long, elu (seven) has a long e but entu (eight) a short one, and hattu, ombattu have a doubled t.

The number comes before the noun, as in English. For things, the noun usually stays in the singular after a number: ಎರಡು ಟೀ (eradu tee) 'two teas', ಮೂರು ಮನೆ (mooru mane) 'three houses'. The plural ending -galu is possible (mooru manegalu) but is not needed in speech.

ಒಂದು (ondu) also does the work of 'a/an' when you want to stress 'one': ondu tee kodi, 'a tea, please'.

ಎಷ್ಟು (eshtu) asks both 'how many?' and 'how much?'.

guide.title: Counting people: special forms
guide.text:
Kannada counts people differently from things. For one and two people there are special words:

one man: ಒಬ್ಬ (obba); one woman: ಒಬ್ಬಳು (obbalu); one person, respectfully or when gender does not matter: ಒಬ್ಬರು (obbaru).

two people: ಇಬ್ಬರು (ibbaru).

Saying ondu or eradu for people is a typical learner's mistake: 'two children' is ibbaru makkalu, not eradu makkalu.

From three upwards the everyday way is the ordinary number plus ಜನ (jana, 'people'): mooru jana, naalku jana, hattu jana. Written Kannada also has ಮೂವರು (moovaru, three people) and ನಾಲ್ವರು (naalvaru, four people), which you will meet in reading.

guide.title: Kannada digits and zero
guide.text:
Kannada has its own digits: ೦ ೧ ೨ ೩ ೪ ೫ ೬ ೭ ೮ ೯. You will see them on bus number boards, calendars, some shop signs and government papers, so it is worth learning to recognise them - especially ೧ (1), ೨ (2), ೩ (3) and ೫ (5) for bus numbers. International digits are used just as often.

Zero is ಸೊನ್ನೆ (sonne). Phone numbers are read digit by digit, usually in English, but you will hear sonne, ondu, eradu too.

phrases.note: Numeral: ೭. The e is long, and the l is the retroflex ಳ.
For people, not ondu. obba for a man, obbalu for a woman, obbaru when being respectful.
The noun stays singular after a number.
